prize_parts.citation: for showing how collateral constraints and asset prices amplify and propagate shocks into persistent credit cycles

statement.case_for: Kiyotaki and Moore (1997) isolate a single, tractable mechanism: borrowing limits tied to collateral values feed back on asset prices and so amplify and propagate small shocks. The insight is conceptual, not just widely cited. It underlies balance-sheet and financial-friction models, crisis analysis and macroprudential thinking, and it is a contracting idea at heart: enforcement limits determine what can be financed. About 30 years of theory, quantitative work and crisis-era experience have left the mechanism standard. Hearing colleagues, I now think the cleanest credit is the two originators. The opening support is also not a measure of merit. I still rank this first on the substance of the idea and its durability, while recognising that B010 has the broadest agreement and an equally clean attribution.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is overlap with the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises, which could make a collateral-constraint prize look like a second award for one theme. Direct empirical identification of the amplification channel is also weaker than the theory's influence suggests. The financial-accelerator strand of Bernanke, Gertler and Gilchrist is closely related, so a narrow two-name citation leaves out a major contributor. B010 has a mature, well-confirmed empirical record and unusually uniform attribution, and I take seriously that it may be the safer case.

responses.point: Teorell argues that the 1997 Kiyotaki-Moore paper makes a clean two-person attribution, and that Gertler and Gilchrist extend and build on the framework, with Bernanke's earlier recognition complicating a broader group.
responses.response: This moves me. In my opening I proposed adding Gertler, but his strongest claims lie in the accelerator, banking and intermediation extensions, which is where the 2022 overlap and his presence on B037 create the most credit ambiguity. I now prefer the two originators. I still read the two lines as complementary, so I would not describe Gertler's contribution as derivative. Our disagreement is about citation boundaries, not about how important the accelerator is.

responses.point: Krusell ranks B037 first, as the working core of monetary policy, but notes the field is crowded and that three names cannot capture Calvo, Taylor, Woodford, Gali, Christiano, Eichenbaum, Smets and Gertler. He ranks Kiyotaki-Moore third and limits it to the two originators because of the 2022 overlap.
responses.response: I agree with Krusell's attribution concern about B037, and it is a main reason I keep it out of my preferred configuration. A prize for a collective synthesis would force a contestable three-name cut, and he concedes this himself. I also accept his two-originator limit for B019. Where I differ is on ranking: the central-bank influence of B037 is large, but B019 is a single identifiable discovery with a clean credit line, which I weigh more heavily under common criteria across fields.

responses.point: Hassler ranks B010 first and proposes Kiyotaki, Moore and Gertler on B019 at fourth. He worries that overlap with Bernanke's 2022 recognition lowers perceived novelty, and that Gilchrist's and Bernanke's claims complicate selecting three names.
responses.response: Hassler's novelty point is the main substantive objection I share. My response is that 2022 rewarded work on the role of banks and on runs and crises, whereas Kiyotaki-Moore concerns collateral values and asset-price feedback in the real economy. They are distinct mechanisms, though the committee should weigh the thematic adjacency. His difficulty in choosing three names is a further reason for me to move to two. I also accept that his first-place ranking of B010 reflects a legitimate view that a mature, well-validated field-level advance deserves priority.

responses.point: Boppart ranks B019 first with the two originators, and excludes Gertler and Gilchrist to keep credit on the originating mechanism because of the overlap with Bernanke's recognition.
responses.response: I agree on the two-name boundary and the maturity assessment. His uncertainty about whether the accelerator strand should share credit is real and I do not think it is fully resolved. I do not treat the agreement among members who ranked B019 first as additional evidence of merit; it only shows that we read the same papers similarly.

uncertainties: Whether the committee sees the collateral-constraint mechanism as distinct enough from the 2022 banking-and-crises prize.
Whether excluding Gertler and the accelerator strand (with Gilchrist and Bernanke) leaves an unacceptable gap in the citation.
How strong direct empirical identification of the amplification channel is, relative to B010's firm-level evidence.
Whether B010 should take priority because it combines broad agreement with clean attribution; I am not fully settled on the order of B019 and B010.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. I am a corporate-finance specialist, which gives me field proximity to B019 and B008. John Moore's incomplete-contracting work is intellectually adjacent to my financial-contracting research. No co-authorship, institutional tie or other personal connection to any candidate on the shortlist is apparent from the profile. I hold an adjunct appointment at Chicago Booth, but no candidate affiliation is recorded.
